title: Set apart (Acts 13:1–12)
hookLine: a mixed table, empty stomachs on purpose, and a choice made in the middle of worship
tomorrow: why would anyone be filled with joy right after being run out?

lines: A STOMACH IN A QUIET ROOM.
cards: A stomach growls in a quiet room, and everyone hears it. No vote, no committee, no plan on a whiteboard.
Acts 13 opens with a list of names at the church in Antioch: Barnabas, Simeon that was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
A mixed table, from different places and different households. And a big choice, one that sends the story to sea, arrives while they're hungry on purpose.

teach.b: Here's the line: "As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."

The King James says ministered; other translations say worshiped. Either way, the call comes through the body as much as the mind: voices raised in worship, stomachs empty. They weren't fasting to squeeze out an answer.
They were already worshiping when the word came. And they still don't rush. "And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."

teach.h: HANDS ON SHOULDERS, THEN THE ROAD.
teach.b: More hunger, more prayer, then the weight of hands on two pairs of shoulders, and only then the road. Set apart doesn't mean set above. It means set aside for a job; the rest of the table stays to keep the church going.

The first stop is the island of Cyprus, and the work meets resistance right away. A governor named Sergius Paulus, "a prudent man," wants to hear them, and a sorcerer at his court, Elymas, tries to turn him away.

teach.h: SAUL, WHO ALSO IS CALLED PAUL.
teach.b: Saul, "who also is called Paul," fixes his eyes on him, and Elymas goes blind for a season.
Something to tell a friend tonight: this is where the name Paul enters Acts. Not on the Damascus road. Here, setting out.

how: In some churches, people sent out for a new work, such as missionaries or new ministers, are prayed over with hands laid on them, sometimes after a time of fasting.

o: ranked above others for special holiness
cut off from the group as a punishment
chosen and sent out for a particular work

games.q: Antioch and Cyprus — tap the pairs.
p: ministered to the Lord, and fasted

s: Saul's name changed to Paul on the Damascus road
Acts first says 'Saul, who also is called Paul' here, on Cyprus, at the start of the journey.
the church at Antioch was fasting when the Spirit spoke
as they ministered to the Lord, and fasted.
Barnabas and Saul left the moment the Spirit spoke
the church fasted and prayed again and laid hands on them first.

games.q: your youth group has to choose who leads the food drive, and everyone wants to vote right now. what would Antioch do first?
o: worship and pray together first, then choose.
vote fast, then pray that it works out.
skip the choosing and let whoever volunteers lead.
games.why: the call came as they ministered to the Lord and fasted, and even then they fasted and prayed again before sending anyone.

practice: Pour a glass of water and set it in front of you. For the sit, don't drink: notice the wanting, the dry mouth, the small pull toward the glass, and listen to the room underneath it. When the bell ends, drink slowly, and taste it.

wordCard.voice: Set apart. Barnabas and Saul, named while the church at Antioch worshiped and fasted, and sent out with hands on their shoulders.

orig.note: Greek: separate, set apart, the command in Acts 13:2, separate me Barnabas and Saul.

carryVoice: The line to keep: while they worshiped, because the call came in the middle of it. Until tomorrow.
